title: Why England fans sing "It's Coming Home"
summary: I've seen a lot of comments on social media saying England fans are arrogant and entitled. I always see people saying they'll support any team that's playing against England. They often reference to the song "it's coming home" as proof of our arrogance and entitlement. England have not won a major tournament since 1966. Most of us grew up watching England get knocked out on penalties, lose to red cards, or find some other painful way to fall short. If anything, us English are known for being pretty self deprecating. We hope for the best, but we also expect something to go wrong. "It's Coming Home" was written for Euro '96, when England hosted the tournament. Over the years, it's become less of a prediction and more of an expression of hope. When England fans sing "It's coming home," it's usually not because we genuinely expect to win. It's because, despite decades of disappointment, we still allow ourselves to believe that maybe this time could be different. You don't have to like England or support us, but I do think the song is widely misunderstood outside England. It's much more tongue in cheek and optimistic than it is arrogant. submitted by /u/Hungry-Kale600 [link] [comments]

Yet, when we look back through history, we rarely remember those moments in isolation. Instead, we remember the athletes who stood at the center of them. That reality is both beautiful and unfortunate. Beautiful because every generation is fortunate enough to witness individuals who elevate their sport beyond competition and transform it into something larger than themselves. Unfortunate because the stories, traditions, cultures, and communities that built those sports are often overshadowed by the brilliance of a single star. Time and again, sports become defined not by the game itself but by the athletes who emerge at precisely the right moment. Sometimes a sport finds itself in need of renewal—a fresh face capable of inspiring a new generation of fans. Other times, the world itself is searching for something greater: a symbol of perseverance, humility, excellence, or hope. In those moments, a player can become more than an athlete. They become an archetype. What is fascinating is that this rise to greatness is not always driven by statistics, championships, or records alone. While accomplishments certainly matter, they rarely tell the entire story. History is filled with athletes whose résumés are extraordinary, yet whose impact never extended beyond the boundaries of their sport. Conversely, there are others whose legacy transcends numbers because they captured something far more difficult to measure. They captured the public’s imagination. Sometimes it is the relentless determination of an athlete who refuses to quit. Sometimes it is the grace they display in victory or the dignity they maintain in defeat. Sometimes it is their ability to carry the expectations of millions while remaining remarkably human. And sometimes, it is simply the way they compete—with a passion, integrity, and sportsmanship that reminds us why we fell in love with the game in the first place. The rarest athletes are not those who merely dominate their opponents. They are the ones who remind us that sports can still be a reflection of our highest ideals. They inspire us not because they win, but because of how they pursue greatness. Their story becomes intertwined with the story of the sport itself, and for a brief moment in history, the two become impossible to separate. Those are the athletes who endure long after the final whistle blows. Those are the athletes who become legends. Behind every iconic moment is a lifetime of sacrifice. The athletes who become the faces of their generation do not arrive by accident. Their rise is built upon years of unseen work—the early mornings, the late nights, the injuries, the setbacks, the failures, and the relentless pursuit of improvement when nobody is watching. The public often sees the trophy presentation, the record-breaking performance, or the championship celebration. What they rarely see are the countless moments of doubt and adversity that made those achievements possible. And yet, greatness alone is not always enough to create a legend.
